content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its treatment recommendations for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Treponema pallidum (syphilis), as well as introduced new guidelines for syphilis testing and partner services. These updates are based on systematic reviews and evidence-to-decision frameworks to address the evolving patterns of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Licensing and Usage The WHO publication is available under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent terms. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that the WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation. Background on Treatment Updates The WHO is developing consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care of STIs. The updated recommendations aim to address the increasing resistance to azithromycin and extended-spectrum cephalosporins, particularly in N. gonorrhoeae. The 2016 WHO guidelines considered global and local resistance patterns, but the rise in AMR necessitates updated strategies to mitigate further resistance development. 2016 WHO Recommendations for N. gonorrhoeae Treatment 1. Dual Therapy: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly (IM) as a single dose + Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose + Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. 2. Single Therapy (based on local resistance data confirming susceptibility): Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM as a single dose. Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose. Spectinomycin 2 g IM as a single dose. Updated Evidence and Surveillance Data Ceftriaxone: Resistance to ceftriaxone is increasing globally, though in Europe, where 500 mg doses were introduced in 2013, resistance has decreased. Pharmacodynamic data suggest that 1 g of ceftriaxone can eradicate all strains except highly resistant pharyngeal strains. Cefixime: Resistance to cefixime is decreasing in some countries, but azithromycin resistance is rising. Azithromycin: Resistance to azithromycin has increased significantly in many regions, including Europe, between 2011 and 2020. Treatment Failures and Resistance Patterns Reports of treatment failures with ceftriaxone have been sporadic but are increasing. Higher doses (500 mg to 2 g) have been effective in most cases. Resistance to ceftriaxone and azithromycin is more prevalent among men who have sex with men (MSM) compared to men who have sex with women. Resistance to ciprofloxacin, penicillin, and tetracycline is also high in this group. Adverse Effects and Pain Considerations Higher doses of IM ceftriaxone may cause more pain at the injection site, but no consistent pattern of increased adverse events has been observed with higher doses of ceftriaxone or cefixime. Certainty of Evidence The overall certainty of evidence for the effects of these medications is low due to older studies, small sample sizes, and changes in resistance patterns over time. Recommendations for Future Practice Continued surveillance of AMR patterns is critical to inform treatment guidelines. The WHO emphasizes the importance of using effective antimicrobial regimens to reduce the risk of further resistance development. Ceftriaxone, cefixime, and azithromycin remain in the watch group of antibiotics on the WHO Access, Watch, and Reserve (AWaRe) list, highlighting the need for cautious use. These updates are part of the WHO's broader effort to ensure transparency and provide evidence-based guidance for managing STIs in the context of evolving resistance patterns.
